decisions_2026-09-02.migration_incident: Widening the book_label CHECK to add 'Word Index and Glossary' surfaced a real, live bug from the PRIOR migration (escalation #1382, lifecycle_tag CHECK removal, same session): SQLite's ALTER TABLE RENAME auto-rewrites trigger bodies that textually reference the renamed table -- the rename-old-table-away/create-new/drop-old sequence used for #1382 left prose_section's FTS-sync triggers (prose_section_ai/au) pointing at 'prose_section_type_old', a name that no longer existed the moment that migration committed. Confirmed live: any INSERT/UPDATE on prose_section was broken from the moment #1382 committed until this was caught and fixed (checked: no writes actually occurred in that window, so no data was lost -- FTS row count stayed 949=949 throughout). Fixed by dropping the two triggers before any further rebuild, rebuilding the table, then recreating the triggers fresh against the stable final name -- verified with a live insert/update/delete round-trip confirming FTS sync actually works, not just that the statements execute. See BUILD.md #219 for the full record.

_meta.content_rewrite_2026-09-02: Researcher review: the original heading/body content was wrong in kind, not just in wording -- headings mixed the term with a description ('grain -- the actual rollup unit (supersedes...)'), and bodies were investigative/audit narration (fallout-scan findings, 'not in the original seed list', provenance trivia), not definitions. Rewritten per instruction: heading = the term alone (a bare word, or a word plus a short disambiguating sense-qualifier in parentheses where more than one sense exists in the project -- e.g. 'cluster (M-code)' vs 'cluster (C-code)' -- never a full description). Body = [DEFINITION] (what it means, plus any other terms/spellings for the same thing, folded into the prose) and [BACKGROUND] (provenance, usage, known issues -- only what's actually useful to a reader, not a record of how this scan found it). The 3 contentious entries (cohabitation, role (span classification), owner term) carry a [BACKGROUND -- CONTESTED] section that states the specific tension AND names a concrete check that would resolve it, not just a flag that a tension exists. The parenthetical-sense-qualifier convention for headings (rather than, say, a separate structured disambiguator) is Claude's own interpretation of 'in some cases a multi word term' -- not confirmed against a more literal reading (heading = bare word only, sense kept elsewhere) -- flagged for correction if that reading was intended instead.
_meta.heading_simplification_2026-09-02: Researcher, this chat: "the heading need to be in the form that you can rapidly search and apply it, complex strings make it more difficult to scan the pick of the relevant bits. if needed, rather create two rows and use to description to arbitrate between the terms." Stripped every parenthetical sense-qualifier from headings (e.g. 'cluster (M-code)' -> 'cluster') -- rows that share a bare heading are disambiguated entirely by their own [DEFINITION] text, not by the heading string. 'Gate 1 / Gate 2' (the one heading that packed two terms together rather than one term plus a qualifier) split into two separate rows for the same reason. Entry count now 37 (was 36).

bible_research.prose_section.heading: M-Code cluster
bible_research.prose_section.body:
[DEFINITION] An analytical grouping mechanism for Strong's terms. Each cluster carries an M-code (e.g. M01). M01–M47 group Strong's terms by shared characteristics of the inner being. Two further codes extend the scheme: FLAG holds terms not yet decided into a characteristic grouping, and T2 holds supplementary terms that are not themselves inner-being terms. T3 is a related tier (not itself a cluster_code value) for action verbs and other terms not directly tied to an inner-being operation.

[BACKGROUND] Bare cluster columns holding this sense: ib_characteristic.cluster, verse_span_index.cluster, file_manifest.cluster; the code itself is cluster.cluster_code. See the other "cluster" entry below for an unrelated, retired scheme (C01–C22) that also uses the word "cluster" on one column.

bible_research.prose_section.heading: characteristic
bible_research.prose_section.body:
[DEFINITION] Characteristic (short form Char) is widely used to describe inner being behaviour. It is the foundation for the programme observations of how the inner being works or manifest. The composition and naming of specific characteristics are not predefined and is part of the subject matter of the program. The word_registry.word IS NOT a characteristic and the registry should never be used as the composition of a specific Characteristic. The lemma, gloss, sub gloss or surface word used in the lexical is not synonymous to a characteristic.  A specific characteristic is likely to be associated with a group of strong terms with several of these groupings being part of Cluster. The cluster grouping sits somewhere between the individual strong term and analytical assembly of related terms into a cluster.

[BACKGROUND] Unlike the body that have a defined set of members (arms. fingers etc) , the inner being does NOT consist of a predefined list of characteristics. Characteristics cannot be measured and their structure and existence are only known by inference on the inner being behaviours. Characteristics is not a thing, it is likely to be something like a process, state, movement. The collection of behaviours, processes, actions, movements in the inner being give substance to a specific characteristic such as anger or love. The naming of specific characteristics are still in flux and have not yet been established. Associated words for this grouping effort is clusters, subgroups, phenomena, and family

bible_research.prose_section.body:

[BACKGROUND] Used at two different grains project-wide: the term-level anchor verse (this entry) and the passage-level anchor verse (a maximal run of consecutive verses' first verse). The programme prose also notes hib.first_verse_id "plays an analogous role" for a HIB without being named anchor in the schema — a drafting gap, not a misreading.
